clue.text: Writer whose career began with love and friendship

definitions.text: Writer whose career began with love and friendship

parts.words: Writer whose career began with love and friendship
parts.note: Love and Freindship is a famous piece of teenage juvenilia by the author of Emma, so her career literally began with that title

explanation.surface: A novelist's career was launched by affection and companionship.
explanation.walkthrough: The lower-case 'love and friendship' reads as feelings, but it is the title of an early burlesque written by the novelist at fourteen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Regency novelist's earliest surviving works include the comic epistolary tale Love and Freindship.

clue.text: Bill cupbearer for African writer

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, a bill
Hebe was cupbearer to the Greek gods

explanation.surface: Settle the tab for the waiter who served an author from Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinua Achebe was the Nigerian novelist who wrote Things Fall Apart.

clue.text: His return requested by James Blish

definitions.text: His return requested by James Blish

parts.words: His return requested by James Blish
parts.note: James Blish wrote the science-fiction novel titled with a plea for a man of our planet to come home

explanation.surface: A science-fiction author asks for someone to come back.
explanation.definitionFit: Blish's novel Earthman, Come Home asks a native of our planet to return.

clue.text: No ham for him

parts.note: a ham is an over-the-top performer; the player meant here does the opposite and plays too quietly

explanation.surface: A man who refuses to eat pork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' tempts as meat, but it is theatre slang for an actor who overdoes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer who plays a part too subtly is the opposite of a hammy actor.

clue.text: "They drove in all directions, scattering their ample allowances…" (Thomas Hughes)

definitions.text: "They drove in all directions, scattering their ample allowances…" (Thomas Hughes)

parts.words: "They drove in all directions, scattering their ample allowances…" (Thomas Hughes)
parts.note: a passage from Tom Brown's Schooldays describing young bucks driving a kind of carriage with horses harnessed one before the other

explanation.surface: A quoted line about extravagant youths racing about, from Tom Brown's Schooldays.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word in Hughes's sentence names what the young men drove: two-horse carriages with the horses in line.
explanation.definitionFit: Such carriages, with one horse harnessed ahead of the other, were the fashionable vehicles of reckless young drivers.

clue.text: Christie's fatal river

parts.note: Agatha Christie's mystery Death on the ... is set on an Egyptian river cruise

explanation.surface: The waterway where a crime novelist set a death.
explanation.definitionFit: Christie's novel Death on the Nile makes the Egyptian waterway the scene of murder.

clue.text: Testament read with sad tear for Venetian School madrigal composer

parts.note: a last will and testament

indicators.note: something sad is in a sorry state, so these letters are knocked out of shape

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A will is read out to tearful mourners of a Renaissance musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sad' reads as describing the mourners' tear, but it is the anagram signal giving AERT; 'Testament' is a will, not scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: Adrian Willaert, a Flemish musician, founded the Venetian school and wrote many madrigals.

clue.text: With which I convinced

parts.note: the means of convincing someone is coaxing argument; it is also the title of Austen's last completed novel

explanation.surface: The means by which I won someone over.
explanation.definitionFit: Coaxing argument is the means by which people are convinced, and it also names Austen's final completed novel.

clue.text: One aspect of Wouk work

parts.note: Herman Wouk wrote the novel ..., Outside, whose title names two opposite aspects

explanation.surface: A feature of something Herman Wouk wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: Wouk's novel Inside, Outside has a title of two halves, and this is the first.

clue.text: Irish dramatist who made discovery in 1763

definitions.text: Irish dramatist who made discovery in 1763

parts.words: Irish dramatist who made discovery in 1763
parts.note: Frances, mother of the author of The Rivals, had her comedy The Discovery staged in 1763

explanation.surface: An Irish playwright found something in the eighteenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovery' looks like a find, but it is the title of a 1763 comedy by Frances Sheridan.
explanation.definitionFit: Frances Sheridan, an Irish playwright, had her play The Discovery produced at Drury Lane in 1763.

clue.text: Early aeronautical engineer

parts.note: in Greek myth the craftsman who built wings of feathers and wax for himself and Icarus

explanation.surface: A pioneer of flight.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical Greek inventor made wings to escape Crete, making him the first flight engineer.

clue.text: Appear to notice first manuscript

parts.note: to see is to notice

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word that follows it is taken

explanation.surface: A manuscript seems to catch the eye at first glance.
explanation.definitionFit: To seem is to give an impression or look a certain way, as in appearing.

clue.text: Kipling's police chief seen as post impressionist's doppelganger

definitions.meaning: Kipling's stories feature a police officer of this name in India
Charles of that surname in The Moon and Sixpence is modelled on Gauguin

explanation.surface: A policeman from Kipling is taken for an artist's double.
explanation.walkthrough: Maugham based the painter in The Moon and Sixpence on Gauguin, the post-impressionist.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to Kipling's Indian policeman and to Maugham's Gauguin-like painter.

clue.text: Battle date confused by graduate artist (4-69)

parts.note: the Battle of the Alma was fought in the Crimean War

indicators.note: jumbled, telling us the word date is rearranged

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts

explanation.surface: A painter muddles the date of a battle he graduated in studying.
explanation.walkthrough: The Alma is a Crimean river and battle; 'confused' rearranges the date into TADE, and 'graduate' is the usual degree abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence Alma-Tadema was a Victorian painter of classical scenes.

clue.text: The Browns finished them off

parts.note: Austen left a novel about a family unfinished; Edith and Francis Brown published a completion in 1928

explanation.surface: A family named Brown killed off some people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finished them off' reads as murder, but means completed an unfinished novel about a family.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's abandoned fragment about a family was later completed by Edith and Francis Brown.

clue.text: In pieces cut, the viper still (did swift)

definitions.text: In pieces cut, the viper still (did swift)

parts.words: In pieces cut, the viper still (did swift)
parts.note: Swift's line says a viper chopped up still joins itself back together, the missing verb

explanation.surface: A quoted line by Swift about a chopped-up snake.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb Swift used means to join the severed parts together again.

clue.text: Dun Verne? maybe has confidence destroyed

definitions.note: the clue phrase describes a state; the answer is the adjective for it

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be another arrangement

explanation.surface: A dun-coloured Verne novel may shatter someone's nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shaken and nervous has lost their composure and assurance.

clue.text: Chaps using it to come back to composer

parts.note: chaps are men

indicators.note: the words are read in the opposite direction, coming back on themselves

explanation.surface: Some chaps use it to make a comeback as a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come back' turns the clue's own two little words round together, giving OTTI; the composer is Menotti.
explanation.definitionFit: Gian Carlo Menotti was the Italian-American opera writer of Amahl and the Night Visitors.

clue.text: Somewhat exaggerated character from Measure for Measure?

definitions.meaning: Mistress ... is a brothel keeper in the Shakespeare play

explanation.surface: A rather over-the-top figure from Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means excessive, and also names Shakespeare's bawd Mistress Overdone.

clue.text: Drama writer found in the nursery

parts.note: a drama is a play
a pen is a writer

explanation.surface: A playwright discovered in a children's room.
explanation.definitionFit: The enclosure where a toddler is set to amuse itself is a fixture of a children's room.

clue.text: Home teamplayer who got out (first ball)

definitions.text: Home teamplayer who got out (first ball)

parts.words: Home teamplayer who got out (first ball)
parts.note: sounds like a cricketer out first ball, but describes the pantomime girl kept home who went out to the prince's ball

explanation.surface: A home cricketer dismissed off the first delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batter 'out first ball' is dismissed at once; here the ball is a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy-tale heroine stayed at home slaving, then got out to the royal ball.

clue.text: Considerable verve in Spanish and English articles

parts.note: el is the Spanish definite article
an is an English indefinite article

explanation.surface: Spanish and English articles show a lot of verve.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair and dash are what the word means: spirited style.

clue.text: Handsome sort of verse?

definitions.meaning: beautiful, as in the youth Adonis
a short classical metre of a dactyl and spondee

explanation.surface: A good-looking type of poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means like Adonis, and also names a classical metre.

clue.text: "4th. (— ), In the morn to our own church, where Mr Mills did begin to nibble at the Common Prayer" (Pepys)

definitions.text: "4th. (— ), In the morn to our own church, where Mr Mills did begin to nibble at the Common Prayer" (Pepys)

parts.words: "4th. (— ), In the morn to our own church, where Mr Mills did begin to nibble at the Common Prayer" (Pepys)
parts.note: a Pepys diary entry dated on the Christian sabbath, when he went to church

explanation.surface: Pepys records a Sunday morning church visit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Christian day of worship, Sunday, is called this, as Pepys writes in his diary.

clue.text: Record of Pratchett's world

definitions.meaning: Terry Pratchett's flat fantasy world rests on elephants on a turtle

explanation.surface: An account of the fantasy author's world.
explanation.definitionFit: A vinyl recording is round and flat, like Pratchett's flat world.

clue.text: Set forth suggestion in favour of Ezra?

parts.note: pro means in favour of
Ezra Pound, the American poet

explanation.surface: A proposal championing the poet Ezra Pound.
explanation.definitionFit: To put forward an idea for consideration is to propose it.

clue.text: Some say to paddle canoes is intellectual activity

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are used

explanation.surface: Some claim that paddling a canoe exercises the mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek term is the philosophers' word for the mind's act of understanding.

clue.text: State of Hamlet's father's beard?

parts.note: Horatio describes the ghost's beard as a sable silvered, greying with age

explanation.surface: A question about the condition of a ghost's beard.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoariness or greyness is meant, as in the ghost's silvered beard.
